newsitem.title: FRANCE: Peres says Arafat approved refusal to quit Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Peres says Arafat approved refusal to quit Hebron.

text.p: Former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres said in an interview published on Thursday that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had backed his decision to suspend a promised Israeli troop pull-out from Hebron.

Peres told the French magazine Le Nouvel Observateur that Arafat feared such a withdrawal from the last big town on the Palestinian-run West Bank patrolled by Israeli troops would have meant handing over Hebron to the militant Islamic group Hamas.

After Israel's 1993 peace pact with Arafat's Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), it committed itself to remove its troops from much of Hebron as part of a wider Palestinian self-rule deal, but a March 1996 target date was allowed to lapse.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who defeated Peres in elections last May, said in Washington after a summit with Arafat on Wednesday that he was committed to a withdrawal from Hebron, on condition that Israel's security was also guaranteed.

Following the murder of prime minister Yitzhak Rabin in November, Peres said, Israeli soldiers quit seven cities and hundreds of villages in the West Bank "thanks to which the Palestinians have a territory, an administration, autonomy".
"And then the Hamas attacks took place. But do you know what was the make-up of the Palestinian population in Hebron? Ninety percent of them were controlled by Hamas.

"So I can reveal today that Arafat himself agreed that the Israelis should not hand over Hebron to the Islamic militants. Why? Simply because at that time, the Palestinian authority did not have an organised and efficient police," Peres said.
Hamas launched a wave of bombings in the months following Rabin's murder in an attempt to derail the peace process.
The election of the hardline Netanyahu to replace Peres cast a further pall over peace hopes.

Then an outbreak of widespread, bloody Israeli-Palestinian violence last week prompted U.S. President Bill Clinton hastily to convoke the Washington summit in hopes of saving the peace process from collapse.
Perhaps the biggest sticking point was the question of Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron, where about 400 Jewish settlers live surrounded by 100,000 Palestinians.
The summit ended on Wednesday with few concrete results other than an agreement to resume mid-level Israeli-Palestinian talks.
